utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, you heard this. There was some sort of misunderstanding, so that you will actually see this document on the screen. I thought you would have it in hard copy, but apparently not. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll it up a bit so that we can see the heading of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, this is an order for further operations coming from the VP to 207 command from Kljuc. Can you see the document, Mr. Dzafic?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see number 1. "I hereby order --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, where it says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the English version in front of them and the counsel is reading too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: "With parts of forces of the brigade carry out total blockade, search and mopping up of the area in the sectors of Biljani -- Donji Biljani, Domazeti, Botonjici, Jabukovac, Brkici." Would you agree with me that these are the locations mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you can see on top that the date there is the 9th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in fact, this is an order for combat operations in this sector where the killings at Donji Biljani had been committed; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Would you now please move on to the next page. Let us just look at the signature portion of the document. Can you make it out? Can you see who the commander of this unit was?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, could you please just scroll the text back and -- the part which shows which units were to take part in this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we will do it in a moment but just let's look at this. So the commander of this unit -- the commander was Colonel Samardzija. Did you know that man?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of him?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you knew that he was the brigade commander at the time?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if we take a look at the assignments per unit, we see that there is a reconnaissance platoon, a police platoon.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the police squad from Sanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in this situation the commander of this military unit issues an order, and in fact, he is the commanding officer for the operation described here in this order.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, generally speaking. In fact, this police squad was actually resubordinated to the military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And all the events that occurred during this combat operation and at the time when these units took part in carrying out combat assignments, they were all, in fact, under the control of that unit's commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, yes, but the police commander had a crucial role as well because his proposals and his suggestions would be adopted and accepted by his superior commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What I am talking about and what I am referring to is the combat operations, so the decision on which units to use and so on, the units that were resubordinated to that commander, and he was the one who would decide on which of them were to be use and of course he was responsible for their actions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'm just wondering where this line of questioning is going. This witness is not army at all, and he's been asked a series of questions about the command, the orders that were given in response to an army document and he's not involved in this incident and doesn't have any army experience. I'm just wondering how far this line of questioning is going to take us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this man is an officer -- an officer of the Yugoslav Army in reserve. He had a rank, although he was still a police officer. And I think this is an excellent opportunity to actually go through some of these documents with him, and I don't know if the Prosecutor recalls, but one of the first questions that I put to this witness was whether he had actually gone through training for -- or graduated from a school for reserve officers. And this is just a document that I wanted to show to this document [as interpreted] and have his assistance in showing how this worked, and of course the witness can confirm or disapprove of what I was trying to say -- show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Krgovic, apart from his --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, you are a reserve police officer -- police -- reserve military; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. Apart from his elucidation of what the documents say for themselves, how is the Chamber assisted other than itself reading the -- seeing the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, well, I wanted to provide a foundation for my question -- questions regarding this document, and I wanted to inquire what his knowledge about these -- this event or incident was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, did you have an opportunity to talk to people -- or, rather, when I asked you about this incident, you specified the date of this incident. Did you have any knowledge of this incident in -- of this operation in Donji Biljani and the entire operation and how it was conducted?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did find out from the people who had actually survived this operation on the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, during the mopping up operation these people were captured, rounded up and brought in front of the school building where they were shot; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Generally speaking, yes. As for details regarding this incident, I think the best accounts could be actually given by the people who survived this crime, Semso and Dzafer. They have more information than I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But generally speaking, from what you learned from them and what we can see from this document, this was actually a military operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the order is a military order, but whether it was a strictly military operation or not, I really can't tell. I didn't take part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will tender this document into evidence if there are no objections on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: There's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2D46.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, I apologise for this problem with the documents, but let me ask you this: When you gave a statement to the Prosecution, you said that you found some documents from the Crisis Staff, that you found them in this safe box when you came to Kljuc in 1996.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In early 1996, we found them in the safe box.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you testified -- or, rather, when you gave your statement, that happened in your house in Sanica, as far as I could gather, when these events took place on the 25th, 26th, and 27th. Correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 23rd or 24th until the 1st of June I was there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you could only hear that there were combat operations in the area of Pudin Han and where other operations took place. You could hear the shooting; right? And that's the only evidence that you had. You only heard of artillery shells and so on.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And later on you heard that there had been combat operations; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that later at Manjaca. I heard what happened concerning these incidents that we've discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now I will show you a document which was found. I don't know whether it was you who found it or the group before you, but could we see tab 3 in my binder, please. 2D02-0967, please. This document is dated the 30th of May, 1992. It is a warning by the Kljuc defence command and the Crisis Staff, and the extremists are -- were ordered to stop immediately with the shooting. They were given a 15-minute deadline, and it was stated that women, children, and the elderly were to move out within that 15-minute deadline, and if not complied with, then the artillery would start firing. Now, was this document from the collection that you found or from some other collection of documents?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you really. This is the first time that I see this document with handwritten corrections. And there is a list of documents that were found in that safe box.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that the Kljuc defence command and the Crisis Staff of Kljuc issued such calls for people to surrender weapons and to go away? Was it done?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this. However, at Manjaca I learned from the rumours circulating there that people could move about after they raised a white flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, would you please look at the next document. It's a bit more legible. It's your tab 4, and it's also marked as 1110 on the 65 ter list. The document reads: "Given the increasingly more frequent provocations," then once again they're issuing the ultimatum asking that women, children and the elderly withdraw, they would be forced to start firing. This is one such document, and then I would ask you to look at the next document in your tab 5. I'm interested in the white-flag issue. 65 ter number is 1112. It's an order from Prhovo, and the white flag is mentioned in that document.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the white flag is being mentioned there. You said just a minute ago that people who raised the white flag could move about.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that at Manjaca from individuals who spoke about it. They went from one family house to another family house, and they were allowed to do that after they had raise the white flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now tender these documents into evidence if there are no objections on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: There's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibits 2D47, 2D48, and 2D49.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Another question, Mr. Dzafic. As far as I could gather, you were an artillery officer; right? Please remind me. Reserve officer. The school that you graduated from in Zadar was the school for reserve artillery officers, was that what it was, in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you must know that when artillery fire is being opened against a settlement, in accordance with the laws of war, a warning should have been issued to civilians to leave the area; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had no experience in that, but in principle that's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise. Mr. Dzafic, the Prosecutor showed you a document, that's OTP tab 34. 65 ter number is 831. So the Prosecutor showed you these names, the names of the prisoners. I will be putting questions to you concerning the first page of the document, where Vinko Kondic informs Banja Luka -- or, rather, the CSB in Banja Luka and says: "In the territory of our municipality there are no camps, prisons, or collection centres." Do you know whether this is true, this piece of information?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue here is what do they mean when they say "collection centre." If a collection centre is what existed in the gyms of various schools, then there were collection centres and people were kept there for two or three days, but if they mean places like Manjaca under collection centre, then no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I say "collection centre," I mean places where you and your compatriots were held. So when Vinko Kondic says that there were no such places, no collection centres, that that was not true; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen, the date here is the 29th of August. At that point in time, I had been in Manjaca for quite a long time. However, from the minute I was arrested and imprisoned, I was first imprisoned at the gym in Sanica. I was held there for 24 hours. Then I was detained at the gym in Kljuc again. And then the third gym was at Sitnica, where I spent some five to seven days. I'm not sure. I'm not sure because I had been beaten so severely that I was unconscious for some period of time. And then we were taken on foot to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So as far as you know, in Kljuc, were there any such locations where detainees were held, regardless of what we call those names at the time -- what we call those locations.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was arrested, detainees were mostly held at the gym in Kljuc and in the premises of the police station if Kljuc. So there were people both at the gym in Kljuc and the police station in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And after you were brought to Manjaca, there were people coming to Manjaca from Kljuc after you had arrived; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In smaller numbers and in smaller vehicles people were being brought to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzafic. When you were interviewed -- or, rather, you gave several statements while you were in Kljuc. You gave a statement to a representative of the public security centre. His name was Vasic or something like that. And you also gave statements to officers, to soldiers. You mentioned somebody called Mile Dragovic who wore a captain's uniform when he took a statement from you.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was: I gave my first statements -- statement at the elementary school in Kljuc to Mr. Vasic. Nedeljko, I think. He took a statement from me. And then after an hour or two on this same day, on the same morning, gave a statement to a military person who was a captain. As I was giving that statement, Milicevic Dusko was present in the room. He used to know him well. He was a police inspector from Banja Luka. Milicevic Dusko, nicknamed Cadjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And he wore a military uniform with a captain rank.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wore a uniform and the rank was that of a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript: So Milicevic Dusko wore a military uniform and had the rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, or perhaps lieutenant. But at any rate, it was a military uniform, and he was either a captain or a lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And at that time when you went to Manjaca, in a part of your statement you said that you had seen that Stojan Zupljanin came to Manjaca in late July. Do you remember that in your statement? It's on page 23 of your statement. Do you remember stating that?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. I knew Mr. Zupljanin personally, and I remember that. It was either in late July or early August. He came to Manjaca, to the camp at Manjaca, and there were people accompanying him. I saw him only in passing, because the prisoners from the other stable -- or, rather, from stable number 2, whose head I was, were going to take their meals. That was lunchtime. And given the previous experience and given what had happened in the camp prior to that, I didn't dare look around. I didn't dare see who was there. We normally were under orders to keep our hands behind our backs and to stare at the ground or else there would be beating, torture, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you said so at the time. You said that he was in a uniform, and later on you corrected yourself, stating that he wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he wore civilian clothes, but you know the situation that I was in at the time. I was afraid. It was summertime. I really wasn't paying attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that was the only time that you saw or heard Stojan Zupljanin visiting Manjaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then on page 23 you say that you heard from Fahrudin Krivic, that Mirsad Latic approached Zupljanin and that Zupljanin placed his hand on his shoulder, and he said to the commander of the camp, "Had it not been for this man I wouldn't be alive today." Do you remember stating that?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember those words of Mr. Krivic very well. He was on duty at the stable number 2. And after the visit of Mr. Zupljanin to Manjaca, he told me that, and I knew Mirsad personally, the Mirsad you are mentioning now. He was a policeman from Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is that Fahrudin Krivic told you that Mirsad Latic had told him about that conversation; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Mr. Zupljanin left Manjaca, Mirsad told this to Krivic, and Krivic said this to me, because we could have regular contacts with people who were on duty in other stables because we had to communicate in order to coordinate lunch-hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's all I wanted to clarify. I apologise for this. I have a document here. My colleague Mr. Zecevic asked you about this. It's a document about the activities and problem in the functioning of the campaign entitled "Check-point 91." Mr. Zecevic asked you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I don't know whether the Prosecutor would object, but I would like this to be shown to the witness so as to round off this topic. This is 1D00-3437. I know it's not on the list but it stems from the question put by Mr. Zecevic. So I would like to explore this, and I would like to refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'm really in Your Honours' hands here. I don't know this document but I see it has a translation, so -- oh, sorry. Perhaps if I could inquire if it has a translation at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do I understand it was a document that was put to the witness yesterday by Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. Mr. Zecevic actually asked him today about this check-point operation and all the check-points in Kljuc at the time, and what I would like to show is a document that mentions this operation. And that's why I want to show it to the document [as interpretation] although it was not originally on the list of documents that I had prepared with this witness. Of course, if you would allow it, and if not I'm in your hands, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As always, Mr. Krgovic, we are looking with excitement to anything coming from your side, but what exactly is the purpose of bringing up the matter of these check-points and the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the point is -- the purpose is this: As far as we understand the position of the Prosecution, these check-points, or whatever we want to call them, were put up by the Serbian side in order to establish control over the territory in Kljuc municipality, and this was an operation at the ministry of Bosnia and Herzegovina level in order to defuse the tensions and to try and return most of the areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and especially the border areas with Croatia, to return them to peace, because war was going -- war was on at the time in Croatia. And that is the only reason why both the Prosecution and the Defence are dealing with the check-points at length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In my recollection, I think Mr. Zecevic actually covered this quite substantially, so I don't see a need for adding anything further to that matter unless you have a new aspect that wasn't raised by Mr. Zecevic this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I just wanted to assist the witness and to confirm his testimony in this respect, but -- if you agree, but if not, that would be it. I've covered all my issues. So, Mr. Dzafic, thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Would Your Honours like me to start re-examination now or? I see we're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: How long do you expect you will be, Ms. Pidwell?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Fifteen to 20 minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may as well begin.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Ms. Pidwell, on reflection, looking at the time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- the time in the LiveNote we have five minutes to go. Perhaps it would be advisable to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before Ms. Pidwell begins her -- her re-examination, my recollection is that -- and my understanding was that counsel for the Defence, especially for Stanisic, was to have, in the course of their cross-examination, tender the cross-examination in the Brdjanin trial for this witness in the same manner as the 92 ter package was tendered by the Prosecution. Was that an oversight or do counsel intend to do it at a later stage or what? What's the position?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps I can assist. Mr. Zecevic had a plane to catch and has -- well, farewelled himself from me, in any event, before -- in the break, but in answer to your question, the cross-examination in the Brdjanin trial was submitted when I tendered the 92 ter package at the beginning of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's there already. Thank you. Thank you very much. Yes, Ms. Pidwell, you may begin your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dzafic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too, and, yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: That's good. Sir, I now have the opportunity just to ask you a few questions which -- to clarify some issues which have arisen during the course of this morning, and I -- I won't take long. Firstly, sir, you were asked some questions at the beginning of this morning by Mr. Zecevic, and I'm referring particularly to page 9 of the transcript, about some -- about the log-books and daily events that we talked about yesterday. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yesterday we discussed the duty log-book, and in addition to that, Mr. Zecevic mentioned also the daily events log-book.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct. And my question, sir, is the daily events log-book, whose job was it to enter the -- the events of the day into that book?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The daily events log-book was the responsibility of the duty officer, duty police officer, who would receive reports or complaints from citizens, and then -- or by telephone, and he would then enter them in the log-book.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And was there ever an occasion when you or your superior, Vinko Kondic, entered entries into that daily log?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was still employed, I did not normally enter anything, any incidents in the daily log-book, nor was it within my competence, but from time to time I would review them to make sure that the events that were recorded had actually been followed through and completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And was it part of Vinko Kondic's role to also review that log-book?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of principle, no, although he was authorised, of course. He had the powers in case he needed to look into some specific incident. He could then look it up in the daily events log-book.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that daily information reports were then compiled from this -- this record of the daily events, and did these daily reports have to be signed by Vinko Kondic or yourself before they were submitted to the Banja Luka CSB?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked this morning - and I'm referring to page 14 of the transcript - about some contradictory orders from the CSB Banja Luka and from Chief Kondic. My question, sir, is: Were you privy to meetings between Kondic and the Banja Luka CSB in the early part of 1992, before you were removed?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't privy to them. I wasn't privy to the meetings at the CSB chief's office and his meetings with the chiefs of the public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did Vinko Kondic have a good relationship with his superiors in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How this question appear from my cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the issue is whether there were contradictory orders from the Banja Luka CSB or from Vinko Kondic to this witness. And my question is, what is the relationship between the two parties who were supposedly issuing these contradictory orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, my question was: Can you comment on the relationship between Chief Vinko Kondic and his superiors in the CSB Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, in reply to some questions I said that there were never any conflicting orders coming from the chief of the CSB in Banja Luka or Chief Kondic. The conflict -- the contradictions were between the chief of the public security station and the orders coming from the authorities in Sarajevo, from the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And could you now please comment on the relationship between Chief Kondic and the CSB Banja Luka, if you're able to.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't attend those meetings, and I cannot really say much about them. I don't know what to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, sir. You were also asked some questions this morning - and I'm now referring to page 19 and 20 of the transcript - about your walk from the gym at Sitnica to Manjaca and about the -- the -- how far away it was. Could you just tell the Tribunal, please, how long that walk took you.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, we set off around 10.00 in the morning, or thereabout. We were lined up at that time. As I said, we were lined five in a row, and we started walking towards Manjaca. We went -- we stopped briefly in two villages for about 15 minutes or so. We were given some water to drink. And then, if I still remember this well, around 5.00 in the afternoon we arrived at Manjaca. Around 5.00 or 6.00 p.m., or thereabout. Now, if we try and translate that into kilometres, I would say that that would have been about 15 kilometres of -- of road that we crossed from Sitnica to Manjaca, and this is just my estimate, rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You were also asked, later in the morning, about the Red Berets when they came to Kljuc. And I'm referring to pages 23 and 24 of the transcript. And I want to now show you a photograph, sir, and see if that assists you in -- to see whether you recognise the uniforms and if you can comment on them in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And I'd like the witness to be shown P98, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to see a photograph?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Are you able to comment on this photograph and assist us in any way with the uniforms or the regiment or anything like that? I know you haven't seen this photograph before, so it may be difficult for you. And if you can't say, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really say anything about the unit itself. I don't really know anything about that. All I can say is that the group of ten or so men who were in Kljuc at the time wore the same type of uniform. They -- and also they had these red berets on their head.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you recall being asked some questions and being shown the statement of Omer Filipovic, that he made, and being asked about a statement like that being standard procedure for citizens or suspects who were arrested?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was the first time that I saw the statement by Mr. -- by Mr. Omer. The heading was -- that we saw on the statement was the usual heading and standard procedure. However, I question the contents of the statement, how true it is and under what circumstances the statement was given, because knowing the circumstances under which I gave my statement and the way it was taken, under what kind of threat, I have no faith whatsoever as to the truthfulness of this statement. Not 5 per cent of it I believe is true. So this is just on paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And, sir, the statement that you referred to that you made, was it also in this form?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement that I made at the elementary school building in Kljuc and the statement that I made in Sitnica at the elementary school building or at Manjaca, these statements were never shown to me. I never signed them, so I can't really comment on it. I've never seen it -- I've never seen them nor signed them, nor was I ever shown anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And, sir, did Omer Filipovic go in the same group as you to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: There's just one point I want to clarify at page 39 of the transcript. Sir, you were asked a question by Mr. Krgovic, and the question reads: "And the event when the convoy in Busija was attacked, you learned of it one or two hours later from Dragan Tomic, squad commander." And then your answer was that you spent several days in Sanica before you went to Kljuc, and that you'd met up with the commander of the police squad in Sanica. I just want to clarify, sir, the name of the squad commander you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I'd like to clarify something here. On that day when this incident occurred in Busija, close to Kljuc, on the main road between Kljuc and Bosanski Petrovac, I was in Sanica, and it was on that very day that I intended to go back to Kljuc. In Sanica, near a cafe, I ran into a squad commander in Sanica, Milan Tomic. His task was to inspect all the cafes and order them to be shut down because of this incident that occurred in Busija. I asked him if one could get to Kljuc and he said no, the road is blocked off until further notice. So I remained in Sanica. I believe this was on the 27th of May, when all this was happening. I stayed in Sanica until the 1st because the road was blocked and I couldn't return to Kljuc, but, rather, on the 31st, I think in the morning, I was arrested in the house of one of my brothers where I was staying.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You were asked later on this morning by Mr. Krgovic about what you knew about the incident at Biljani, and you talked about how people had told you about that incident when you were at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was told about this at Manjaca. People told me about it. And now looking at this order and seeing all the units that took part in this operation, it became much clearer to me, I mean, what was going on then and what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. My question is: The people that you spoke to about this incident who you say had survived this operation, were they -- what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Muslims. They were of Muslim ethnicity, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And were they, to your knowledge, soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were all civilians. They were detained, arrested in the morning, taken from their homes and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked some questions, sir, by Mr. Krgovic, and I'm referring to page 51 of the transcript. You were shown some documents, some orders which referred to a white flag. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that, and I read those two documents that related to the white flag. As for me, all I knew -- all the information that I had was that the white flag was raised if you were -- would mean that you had surrendered and that you could move freely outside of your home or that place, that village.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was there any other restriction on movement in Kljuc at this time?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to my knowledge, the other active-duty policemen who remained in Kljuc and who hadn't been arrested and taken to Manjaca, they were told and ordered to stay in their homes. Their movement was restricted. It was prohibited. And if necessary, I can tell you the names of those police officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: That's not necessary. Thank you, sir. But I'd ask you to look at a document, please. It's 65 ter 2406. You'll have to look at it on the screen, sir, I think, because it won't be in the binder. Are you familiar with the contents of that order, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How is it related with my cross-examination, Your Honour? It's a document from the 5th of May, and even --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: -- in Kljuc. Ask about what was happening in Kljuc in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, the questions are directly related to the series of questions put by my learned friend about citizens being restricted, their movement being restricted in Kljuc at the time. He put questions about orders that they had to raise a white flag in order to move freely around the town, and this stems from this, that there were other restrictions as well in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In combat operation zone. It's not restriction. My question was related to the warning issued by command of the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, aren't you going beyond where Mr. Krgovic went in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: With respect, sir, I don't think Mr. Krgovic limited his questions to combat zones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But in any event, the result would be that you're opening new ground with this witness, isn't it? And does it -- at the end of the day, what turns on it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, sir, the -- the series of questions from the Defence were that citizens who wanted to move around were able to by raising this white flag, and there was a military order to that effect. The series of questions that preceded these documents didn't restrict that to a combat zone. This witness was in the area at the time, and there was an order restricting the movement of citizens as well at that time, and that's, in my submission, enough proximity to be able to put this to the witness at this stage in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, my question was: Are you familiar with the -- the terms of this order dated 5 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see. I cannot read the order. I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Perhaps I can read it to you, sir, and the interpreters can interpret it. It's an order dated the 5 May 1992, and it reads: "Pursuant to the decision by the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, the president of the Council for Territorial Defence of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly issued the following order: "1. All organs of social communities, economic and other organisations shall immediately begin work under wartime organisation. "2. The entire territory of the Municipal Assembly shall be placed under curfew between the hours of 2200 and 0500, except the persons with official authorisation from the police, military police, or Serbian territorial army. "3. This order shall enter into force immediately." And it's signed by Jovo Banjac, president of the Council for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this order, and I didn't see it but I know and I recall it vividly that there was a curfew imposed at this time as mentioned under item 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I wonder if I can seek to tender that as an exhibit at this stage. I appreciate the difficulties, Your Honour. The witness doesn't know the order was -- well, he was present at the time the order was made and knows that it existed. Of course he's not privy to the document itself or the order itself. I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What he has said is that he is familiar with the fact that there was a curfew. Do you need more than that? I don't see how this can be tendered through him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, if it can be MFI'd at this stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Pending? Pending what?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Pending a further witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document P979, marked for identification. The exhibit number is P979, marked for identification, and the 65 ter, 2406.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And I just have one final topic to cover with you, sir. You were asked some questions - and I'm now referring to line 54 of the transcript - about a person by the name of Dusko Milicevic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that gentleman very well, because we studied together at the Faculty of Political Science in Zagreb. In addition to that, I remember him from before 1991 or 1992. He was a member of the municipal secretariat in Banja Luka where he was an inspector in charge of thefts. He occasionally came to Kljuc to help. That usually happened on Saturdays because Saturday is the market day in Kljuc, when there were some incidents of pick-pocketing, because the citizens who came to the market were targeted by the pick-pockets.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: My question, sir, is, you have said in evidence that he was a police inspector from Banja Luka, and you've also said that he had the rank of a captain or lieutenant and wore a military uniform. Do you know whether he was part of the MUP or whether he was part of the military?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I said when I knew him before the date when I was arrested, that is to say, taken prisoner and brought to the primary school in Kljuc, before that he was discharging the duties which I just described, and at that time I saw him in a military uniform with the rank captain, I think. It was rather captain than lieutenant, but I'm not 100 per cent certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions for you, and I thank you for giving your evidence today, and Their Honours will shortly address you and excuse you from testifying -- or excuse you from court today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We thank you, sir, for coming to testify. You're now released as a witness. We are especially mindful of the -- your experiences and we are grateful for your willingness to relive this unfortunate part of your life to come and testify and assist the Tribunal. Thank you, sir, and we wish you a safe journey back to your place of residence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The court upon its rising will, as the counsel would recall, resume on the 15th of February. And according to the court calendar, which of course is always subject to change, we will resume in this courtroom at 2.15, on the afternoon of Monday, the 15th of February. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 15th day of February, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
